summary: A survey of congestion control approaches for gateways, written to encourage discussion and experimentation. It covers Source Quench, Random Drop, Congestion Indication (DEC Bit), and Fair Queueing. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When too many cars hit a road, there is a traffic jam. This reviews ideas for telling drivers to slow down.

questions: what are gateway congestion control approaches
what is congestion collapse in the internet
how does random drop congestion control work
how does fair queueing prevent congestion
what is the dec bit policy
subtitle: Approaches and mechanisms for controlling packet congestion in Internet gateways.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, gateways experienced congestion that slowed or halted traffic. TCP and ICMP had minimal congestion handling mechanisms. By 1991, several competing approaches existed (Source Quench, Random Drop, Congestion Indication, Fair Queueing), each with different trade-offs, and implementors had no agreed standard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys five major gateway congestion control policies: Source Quench (sending ICMP messages to slow senders), Random Drop (discarding packets probabilistically to signal congestion), Congestion Indication using a bit flag (DEC Bit), Selective Feedback (applying the bit only to heavy users), and Fair Queueing (maintaining separate output queues per source-destination pair). It analyzes fairness, overhead, and how each responds to users running the Slow-start TCP algorithm.
tldr.outcome: No single mechanism was endorsed as best, but the survey laid groundwork for later adoption of Random Drop variants and Explicit Congestion Notification. Slow-start became mandatory for TCP, providing the complementary end-system control mechanism. Gateway congestion control remains an unsolved problem requiring both gateway policies and cooperative end-systems.

today: RFC 1254 is an Informational survey and has not been obsoleted. It documents the state of gateway congestion control in 1991 before Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) was standardized. Today, TCP implementations still use Slow-start, but explicit congestion feedback via ECN (RFC 3168) provides a more efficient alternative to packet loss as a congestion signal. The broader insights about fairness, timescales, and the role of end-system cooperation remain relevant to modern networks.

sections.title: The Congestion Problem
sections.content:
In 1986 and 1987, the Internet experienced congestion collapse: multiple sites simultaneously lost network service for extended periods. The issue was that TCP and ICMP (the Internet Control Message Protocol) had only primitive congestion handling. TCP used a simple sliding window to match the receiver's buffer capacity, but this did not prevent overflowing a gateway's buffers. ICMP offered Source Quench, a message asking a sender to throttle back, but it was rarely effective.

As Internet applications grew more data-intensive (scientific computing, file transfers, and later the Web), gateway congestion became a chronic obstacle. Unlike the receiver's buffer, a gateway's buffer is shared by all traffic passing through it. When demand exceeds a gateway's capacity for processing packets, buffering them, or transmitting them on outbound links, packets are dropped. By the time packets are dropped, the gateway is already congested. The problem is especially acute because the Internet is connectionless: there is no admission control, and any host can send packets at any rate.

The IETF Performance and Congestion Control Working Group surveyed existing and proposed mechanisms to stimulate discussion and experimentation. The goal was not to pick a winner but to document the landscape and clarify the trade-offs so implementors could make informed choices.
sections.eli5: In the mid-1980s, too much traffic hit the Internet at once and it stopped working. Internet routers (called gateways) had no good way to tell everyone to slow down. This document looks at different ideas for fixing the problem.

sections.title: What We Want to Optimize For
sections.content:
An effective congestion policy must balance conflicting goals. Throughput (how much data gets through) and delay (how long each packet takes) are always in tension: maximum throughput comes at the cost of long queues and high delay, while minimizing delay means underutilizing the network. A single metric called power (throughput divided by delay) helps balance these. The optimal operating point, called the knee, is where power is maximized. Below the knee, the network has spare capacity. Above it, congestion increases faster than throughput, so power decreases.

Gateway policies must measure their own performance at the right timescale. If measurements are taken too frequently, they react to random fluctuations. If too rarely, they miss changes and use obsolete information. The RFC discusses two approaches: basing measurements on round-trip time (the time for a packet to leave a sender and an acknowledgment to return, reflecting the end-to-end delay each user experiences) and analyzing the queue regeneration cycle (watching when the gateway queue goes from idle to busy and back). Different users have different round-trip times, so the gateway's measurement interval must accommodate this variation.

Fairness is a key goal when multiple users share a gateway. If all users have equal demand, each should receive an equal share of the gateway's capacity. In practice, demand varies, and identifying each user's fair share is hard. The RFC defines maximally fair allocation as giving each user at least their fair share, with unused capacity distributed to others who want it.
sections.eli5: A good congestion system has to get a lot of data through (throughput) without making packets wait too long (delay). It also has to be fair: if one person sends a lot and another sends a little, the network should not starve the person sending less. And it has to notice congestion at the right time, not too fast and not too slow.

sections.title: Five Gateway Congestion Control Policies
sections.content:
Source Quench (ICMP): When a gateway's buffer overflows, it drops the packet and may send an ICMP Source Quench message back to the sender asking it to slow down. This is the existing Internet standard, but it has severe drawbacks. Different gateway manufacturers implement it differently, so a sender receiving a Source Quench cannot tell how serious the congestion is. Packets from low-bandwidth, intermittent users are dropped disproportionately often because they do not maintain constant queue occupancy. The RFC notes that Source Quench is at best a congestion recovery mechanism (after packets are already being dropped) rather than avoidance (preventing congestion before it starts).

Random Drop: Instead of dropping the last packet to arrive (which can be unfair), this policy drops a randomly selected packet from the incoming traffic. The hypothesis is that a randomly selected packet belongs to a high-demand user with probability matching that user's share of traffic, so heavy users lose more packets than light users. This gives fair feedback and requires only low computational overhead (important for high-speed gateways). Random Drop can be used for congestion recovery (dropping only when buffers overflow) or avoidance (dropping at an increasing rate as the queue grows). The downside is that users on long paths experience exponentially more packet loss if multiple gateways along the path use Random Drop.

Congestion Indication (DEC Bit): Developed at Digital Equipment Corporation for their network architecture, this policy sets a single bit in the header of packets being forwarded whenever the average queue length is high. Instead of dropping packets or sending separate messages, the gateway marks the packets themselves with a congestion flag. The sender or receiver (depending on the protocol) adjusts its sending window in response. This is efficient (low overhead, uses one header bit) and works well for window-based transport protocols. However, it treats all users the same and does not distinguish heavy from light senders.

Selective Feedback Congestion Indication: An enhancement to the DEC Bit policy that tracks each user's traffic separately and sets the congestion bit only for users sending more than their fair share. The gateway keeps counts of packets from each source-destination pair and computes a fair share using a min-max algorithm. This is fairer but requires the gateway to track many users and may have high processing overhead at backbone routers. Aggregating users (for example, treating all traffic from one host as one user) reduces overhead but can penalize low-bandwidth users (like TELNET connections) that share a path with high-bandwidth users (like FTP).

Fair Queueing: Rather than a single queue, maintain separate output queues for each source-destination pair. Service the queues round-robin so each pair gets equal capacity. When a queue overflows, drop from the longest queue. A user that sends more than its share fills its own queue but does not interfere with others. The RFC describes two variants: Bit-Round Fair Queueing (ensuring that long packets do not gain unfair advantage) and Stochastic Fairness Queuing (using a hash function to approximate per-pair queueing with lower memory and processing cost). Fair Queueing scales better with users than Selective Feedback and insulates users with different congestion control policies from each other, but requires storing per-flow state.
sections.eli5: Source Quench says slow down. Random Drop drops some packets to signal congestion. The DEC Bit marks packets to say the network is busy. Selective Feedback marks only the packets from people sending too much. Fair Queueing gives each conversation its own waiting line so one person cannot take over the whole road.

sections.title: How End-Systems Respond: Slow-start and Beyond
sections.content:
Gateway congestion control alone does not reduce demand; it only signals congestion. For the signal to help, hosts must respond. Slow-start, developed by Van Jacobson and standardized in RFC 1122 as mandatory for all TCP implementations, is the key end-system mechanism. Slow-start observes that when a sender first connects or has not sent in a while, it should probe carefully to learn the network's capacity. It starts with a small sending window and doubles it each time a full round-trip completes without packet loss. When loss is detected (timeout or duplicate acknowledgments), it cuts the window in half and resumes probing more slowly. Slow-start adapts the sender's demand to the current state of the network.

The RFC notes that Slow-start works best with a complementary gateway congestion avoidance mechanism such as Random Drop or Congestion Indication. Slow-start reacts to packet loss or congestion signals by backing off, which can take a full round-trip time to take effect. A gateway congestion avoidance policy that drops packets earlier (before buffers overflow) gives Slow-start a chance to react before congestion becomes severe.

End-System Congestion Indication is another approach mentioned: if the network marks packets with a congestion bit, the destination can feed this back to the sender (in TCP ACKs), allowing the sender to adjust its window without waiting for a timeout. This is more responsive than inferring congestion from packet loss.
sections.eli5: Slow-start is how TCP on computers responds to congestion signals. When a connection starts, it sends slowly and speeds up gradually. If packets get lost, it slows down again. It is like a driver accelerating carefully onto a crowded road, speeding up if things flow smoothly, and braking if traffic jams appear.

sections.title: Challenges and Limits
sections.content:
A critical unresolved problem is what happens when non-cooperating hosts do not respond to congestion signals. If a host ignores Source Quench, does not implement Slow-start, or does not respect congestion indication bits, it will send at a constant high rate regardless of network conditions. With Random Drop, a non-cooperating user can monopolize bandwidth by simply increasing the sending rate. Selective Feedback and Fair Queueing can isolate non-cooperating users from cooperating ones, but at the cost of higher gateway complexity. The RFC concludes that addressing non-cooperation is a subject for future research and that administrative action (rate-limiting or blocking misbehaving hosts) may be necessary.

Another limit is that gateway congestion control cannot solve resource exhaustion. If demand persistently exceeds total network capacity, dropping packets or slowing users will not create new bandwidth. Only increasing link capacity or routing traffic away from congested links (a separate problem outside the scope of this RFC) can fully address persistent congestion. The document also notes that network management support (measuring queue lengths and congestion metrics) is needed to deploy and tune these policies effectively, but standard management information bases for this purpose do not yet exist.
sections.eli5: The main problem is that some computers might not listen to congestion signals and just keep sending fast. Another problem is that no one has written down how to actually measure congestion in routers so that network administrators can tune the system. And the biggest problem is that if everyone wants to send more data than the roads can carry, no trick will fix it.
